moorcock_landlord.text: Welcome in, you look like you have walked a fair way. The North York Moors will do that to a person.
The National Park was made in 1952, and it holds one of the biggest stretches of heather moorland in England.
In August and September the whole moor goes purple. There is also an ancient road across Wheeldale Moor, called Wade's Causeway. Folk long said it was Roman, but nobody is quite sure.

then.text: One is plenty, or I will have none for the Sunday crowd. Off with you.

else.text: Here, a Yorkshire pudding. It is eaten first with gravy, to fill you up so you want less beef. Tradition, and good sense.

then.text: Nine pairs of curlew on Moor Farm this spring, where I found five. I am not saying it is the sheep. I am saying it is not nothing.

else.text: Still counting. Curlew numbers on the moors are down, and every nest that gets off is a small argument won.

then.text: Whatever Dale chooses, I will be counting on his hill come April. A farmed moor and a watched moor are both better than one nobody walks.
Tell Dale it is his hill and his say. I would just like him to know the offer is a real one.

else.text: I count birds on contract, which means I am paid in flasks of tea. Curlew, lapwing, golden plover on the tops. All of them are fewer than they were.

The estate has offered Moor Farm a scheme: payments for fewer sheep, drains blocked, heather left to grow. It is not charity. It is a modest, steady income for fifteen years, and in return the moor does what a moor does.

I would like to see it signed, and I would be lying if I said I was neutral. But a hill with nobody living on it is a hill with nobody watching it. A farmer paid to farm for the birds still has to be a farmer.
Hefting survives, by the way. Fewer sheep means a thinner flock, but it is the same flock. Dale would keep his own.
Do not mind me. I am counting. Curlews are the sound of the moor in spring, and there are fewer each year.

then.text: That was the last of yours. I have the whole moor's post to get round, and a pasty to finish.
There you are. A letter for you, care of the Moorcock. I have kept it out of the rain.
Dear {player}. It is the end of April and I am writing this on the back of a feed bill, because the kitchen table is covered in lambing kit.

We lost eleven ewes in the March snow and Dad has not said I told you so, which is how I know he was worried. The rest scanned better than he feared, and the vet said nothing, which I am told is a compliment.
I kept the Leeds job two days a week from this table, which I did not know a job could do. The money is thin. The hill is not.
Thank you for being the one who said it out loud. Dad would not have asked and I would not have offered. Come and see the lambs. P.S. Dad has taught me to say 'gimmer' without laughing.
Dear {player}. Dale here. I am writing from a flat in the village, which has a bathroom indoors and a view of a wall.
Joe took the flock in March and drove them up himself. They went back to their own bit of hill without being told. I wept, and I blame the wind.
The house is let to Joe's shepherd, who is a decent lad and puts his boots in the porch. Hannah rang. She was kind about it, and that was worse.
I am up at the Moorcock most days now, and at the gate on Sundays. It is a farm. Somebody is still farming it. That has to be worth something.
Dear {player}. The scheme man came in February with a clipboard and a good flask. I signed.
We run forty ewes on the hill now instead of a hundred and thirty, and the heather is coming back thick on the south side. The lass counted curlews in April: nine pairs, where she found five.
The payments cover the rent and not much else. Hannah comes and helps with the lambing, and Joe Hartley says I have gone soft. He is not wrong. He is not right, either.
It is a quiet hill. I find I do not mind it as much as I thought I would.
And a flat cap, brown paper round it. Dale's spare, it says, the one with the sweat stain. And a note on how to bake his mother's parkin. She would want the credit.

else.text: Nothing for you yet. Letters from the dale take their time, and so does the weather. Try after a night's sleep.

w55e_dale_pub.text: I come down for the Yorkshire pudding the landlord is too mean to charge me for.
I go up to the gate on Sundays. They knew me fine the first week. By May they only knew Joe's whistle, which is as it should be, and I will not pretend I like it.
